3911:## 4. Existing plans

### 1.3 Open

**D39 — every discovered group member browses, and none of them can be pulled.**
`NexusDetector` synthesises each member as `host + "/repository/" + name`
(`nexus.go:117`, `nexus.go:156`). Measured against `pic-nexus.spw.dev.wallonie.be`
on 2026-08-10:

| Request | Result |
|---|---|
| `GET /repository/dhi-io-proxy/v2/eclipse-temurin/tags/list` | **200** — the browse works |
| `GET /v2/repository/dhi-io-proxy/eclipse-temurin/manifests/21` | **404** |

The second is the path the Docker client builds from that same URL: it puts
`/v2/` first and the whole repository path after it. So the tags table fills
correctly and `p` on any row of it cannot work — the one produces a reference the
other cannot resolve.

It is not a matter of picking a better format string. Which of the four
addressing forms applies is a per-repository Nexus setting, and on this instance
the endpoint carrying it answers 403; the evidence and the design are in
[§3.18](#318-a-registry-member-is-an-address-not-a-url--repo_prefix). Until then
a member row is honest about tags and silently wrong about pulls, which is the
worse half — nothing on screen says the reference will not resolve.

Not reached before now because discovery had never succeeded against a group here
(the same 403), so no member row had ever been rendered.

**D40 is fixed** — see §1.1. It was reachable on its own and was fixed on its
own; §3.18 is what would have made it the normal case rather than a way to
misconfigure, and it no longer has to carry that.

**D39 is the only one open**, above. D21 and D36 closed everything that preceded
them; both are in §1.1.

D12, D13 and D14 were all fixed by §3.8 — see "The three defects it closed"
there for what each turned out to be. D14's inverted test failed the moment the
fix landed, which is what the pattern is for, and has been turned around.

**D35 — the "unpulled" count is only as fresh as the last fetch. Mitigated by
§3.17, not closed.** `detectGitStatus` computes it with
`rev-list --count HEAD..@{u}` (`workspaces/entry.go:90`), and `@{u}` is the local
remote-tracking ref. Nothing in DevDesk moved it, so the column read `0` on a
repository forty commits behind.

`s` now does: sync fetches first and always, so a repository it touches — even
one it *refuses* to fast-forward — comes out with a true count. What remains is
that `loadEntries` still does not fetch, and must not: a directory listing that
hits the network on every drill-down is a different defect. So a repository not
synced since the app opened still shows a number nobody has checked. There is
now a way to make it true, and the one feature that acts on it never trusts it —
which is the difference between a lie and a stale reading.

**D34 — the explorer paginated nothing. Fixed.** Every list in
`internal/ui/gitlab/explorer/api.go` was built with `PerPage: 100, Page: 1`, at
five sites, so a group with more than 100 subgroups or 100 projects was silently
truncated: the explorer showed fewer children than it had, and a recursive clone
skipped repositories without saying so.

`listAll` now walks every page and the four list calls go through it — one loop
rather than four copies, which is how one of them would have ended up wrong. It
terminates on `NextPage <= Page` rather than `NextPage == 0` alone: that also
stops a server pointing back at the page just served, and unlike a page cap it
is a bound that cannot cut a legitimate response short. `perPage` is the one
place the 100 is written.

Three tests assert both halves of a group's children and the pull's own walk
follow every page, and were checked against the pre-fix code — all three fail on
it. A fourth pins the runaway guard.

**D25 — status acted on the wrong monitor under a filter. Fixed** by §2 step 6,
which is also what found it. `getSelectedComponentIndex` replayed the sort by
hand and then indexed, but never applied the text filter the rows had already
been through; the SSL branch walked `m.components` by counting, unfiltered the
same way. Under a filter `e` edited and `ctrl+d` deleted a monitor the user was
not looking at. Same family as D24, and the ninth and last copy of the block.
`TestAFilteredSelectionEditsTheRowTheUserSees` was written before the fix and
failed on the old code.

**D24 — workspaces acted on the wrong directory under a filter. Fixed** by §2
step 5, which is also what found it. The rows were filtered and `m.entries` was
not, and every action resolved the cursor against `m.entries` — so under a
filter they acted on whatever sat at that index in the *unfiltered* list.
Filtering five entries down to `empty-dir` and pressing `ctrl+d` asked to delete
`devdesk`. `ctrl+s`, `r`, `enter`, `ctrl+o` and `ctrl+w` were all wrong the same
way. This is the defect class the component was built to remove, stated in its
package doc, and it was live in the one view where the consequence is a deleted
directory. `TestAFilteredSelectionActsOnTheRowTheUserSees` was written before
the fix and failed on the old code.

**D23 — an unreachable repository manager read as "not a group". Fixed** in
§3.8 step 3, which is also what found it. `NexusDetector.fetchRepoMeta` returned
one bare `ok=false` for both "the manager answered no" and "the manager could
not be asked", and `DetectGroup` collapsed both into `nil, nil`. Harmless while
the answer was discarded on every browser open; not harmless once step 3 cached
it, since one unreachable minute would have erased what was last known. The
error now propagates and a failed discovery is not written through.

**D21** also sat in that package but was **independent of §3.8**, and was fixed
without waiting for it — see §1.1.

D20 and D22 are fixed — see §1.1.

D15–D19 were found by the phase 5 pass, were unrelated to §3.8, and are fixed —
see §1.1. Each had been recorded with an inverted test asserting the broken
behaviour; those tests are what failed when the fix landed, and each has been
turned around to assert the fixed behaviour instead.

**D12 — `AuthEnabled` has no effect on browse or discovery. Fixed** (§3.8 step
2); the description below is what it was. The flag is
honoured in exactly three places: the `docker login` fired on form submit, the
`Logged` column, and the URL list `registryLoginStatusCmd` checks. Neither code
path that actually talks to a registry consults it. `submitSearch`
(`browser_keys.go:142`) calls `docker.GetStoredCreds(credURL)`
unconditionally and hands the result to `searchRegistryTagsCmd`;
`detectRegistryGroupCmd` (`commands.go:563`) does the same before calling into
`registrymgr`. A registry the user has marked as needing no authentication will
still have the host's stored credentials sent to it whenever any other registry
on that host has been logged into — which, given that Docker keys credentials by
host, is the normal case for a Nexus instance. This is the defect the
`anonymous` mode in §3.8 exists to make expressible; today there is no way to
say "do not send credentials here" at all.

**D13 — the browser cannot be dismissed while it is resolving.**
`handleKeyMsg` returns `nil` for every key in `browserStateResolving`
(`browser_keys.go:70`), `esc` included, and that state is entered
unconditionally on open whenever any registry is configured. The detections run
concurrently with an 8 s timeout each, so the wedge is bounded at roughly eight
seconds — but it is eight seconds during which the application ignores the user,
on a screen they may have opened by mistake. §3.8 removes the state rather than
the symptom: with members read from config and cache, there is nothing to
resolve and the form renders immediately.

A smaller thing in the same handler, not worth its own entry:
`HandleGroupDetected` matches the incoming result against `reg.URL`, so two
registries configured with the same URL collide and the second result overwrites
the first. The slug introduced in §3.8 is the natural key to match on instead.

**D14 — the registry filter shows a raw URL for group members.**
`registryFilterLabel()` (`browser_tags.go:63`) resolves the active filter by
searching `b.registries`, which holds only the configured top-level entries.
Discovered members are not in that list, so filtering to one falls through to
returning `b.registryFilter` — the full synthesised URL — where every other row
in the same view shows a short alias. The fix follows from §3.8 rather than
preceding it: once members are persisted they are resolvable, and the filter
gains a group level at the same time.

Pinned inverted by `TestAGroupMembersFilterLabelIsStillARawURL`, which asserts
the raw URL today and asserts the configured registry's alias alongside it as
the contrast.

**D21 is fixed** — see §1.1. It was the last entry in this section.

## 2. Technical debt

### 3.21 The last four tables move to `datatable`

Sorti de §3.20 : le correctif du foreground n'atteint que les `datatable`, et
quatre tables n'en sont pas. Elles rendent leur texte dans la couleur par défaut
du terminal, sur laquelle le thème n'a pas prise, et elles ne peuvent pas être
corrigées là où elles sont — c'est la migration ou rien.

| Table | Fichier | Ce qu'elle fait à la main |
|---|---|---|
| Registries (onglet OCI) | `oci_resources/table.go:311`, `layout.go:56` | largeurs, curseur → objet par indice, **deux sources de lignes** |
| Tags du registry browser | `oci_resources/registry_browser.go:124` | largeurs, échange de styles au focus |
| Network inspect | `oci_resources/network_inspect_form.go:21` | largeurs, `SelectedContainer()` indexe `f.containers` |
| Résultats netdiag | `netdiag/view.go:152` | largeurs, **table reconstruite** à chaque mise à jour |

#### Pourquoi ça ne peut pas se régler sur place

`theme.DefaultTableStyles()` ne pose pas de foreground sur `Cell`, et lui en
poser un casserait la ligne sélectionnée de ces tables exactement comme il
casserait celle d'une `datatable` : les cellules sont rendues, puis la ligne
entière passe à `styles.Selected`, dont le reset intérieur referme le
surlignage au milieu. Le seul endroit où la couleur peut être décidée est un
renderer qui sait si la ligne est sélectionnée — et c'est ce que `datatable`
est.

#### Ce que chacune gagne d'autre

- **Rule 122 devient inexprimable.** Aujourd'hui elle n'y tient que par revue.
  Le danger est réel mais **latent** : `membersCell` rend
  `m.spinner.View() + "refreshing"` dans une cellule, et un spinner bubbles par
  défaut n'émet aucune séquence — vérifié, `View()` rend `"⣾ "` — donc rien ne
  bave aujourd'hui. Il suffit d'un `s.Style = …` pour que si.
- **Rule 116 en un seul endroit.** Les quatre recalculent leurs largeurs à la
  main ; `network_inspect_form` va jusqu'à écrire `columns[2].Width = available
  - flexName - fixedIPv4`, ce que le solveur fait pour toutes.
- **`Selected()` ne peut plus mentir.** Trois d'entre elles résolvent le curseur
  en indexant la tranche d'origine. Sans tri ni filtre c'est correct — et c'est
  précisément ce qui rend l'ajout d'un tri dangereux, puisque rien ne signale la
  dépendance.
- **Les résultats netdiag garderaient leur position.** La table y est
  reconstruite (`table.New`) à chaque mise à jour, donc le curseur retombe en
  haut ; `SetItems` ne le déplace que s'il est sorti de la fenêtre.

#### L'ordre, et le seul morceau non trivial

Les trois petites d'abord — network-inspect, tags, résultats netdiag — qui sont
des colonnes fixes sur une tranche : row type, `Cell`, et les largeurs tombent.

**Registries est le seul cas de forme.** Elle affiche deux populations dans la
même table : les entrées de configuration (`updateRegistryTable`) et les membres
découverts d'un groupe (`updateGroupMemberTable`), avec `←`/`→` entre les deux.
`datatable.Model[T]` est générique sur un seul `T`, donc il faut un type de
ligne qui porte les deux — le patron est `explorerRow`, qui existe pour la même
raison. C'est aussi là que se trouve le `SetStyles` de focus/blur, que
`Focus`/`Blur` portent déjà dans `datatable` (Rule 118).

Non compris : donner un tri ou un filtre à ces tables. La migration doit se voir
uniquement à la couleur du texte.

### 3.18 A registry member is an address, not a URL — `repo_prefix`

Not started. §3.8 gave a group its members; this is about *reaching* one. It
closes D39. D40, which it needed closed with it, was fixed on its own — see
§1.1.

Found on 2026-08-10 trying to browse a single proxy inside a Nexus group. All
measurements below are from that instance — `pic-nexus.spw.dev.wallonie.be`, 64
repositories, 22 of them docker — and every one of them was an anonymous GET.

#### What was measured

Four ways to reach the same image, and no two of them derive from each other:

| Form | `…/tags/list` | What `docker pull` asks for | Pull |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** host, repo `dhi-io-proxy/eclipse-temurin` | 200 | `/v2/dhi-io-proxy/eclipse-temurin/…` → 200 | ✅ |
| **B** host `…/repository/dhi-io-proxy`, repo `eclipse-temurin` | 200 | `/v2/repository/dhi-io-proxy/…` → 404 | ❌ |
| **C** group subdomain, repo `eclipse-temurin` | 200 | `/v2/eclipse-temurin/…` → 200 | ✅ |
| **D** host, repo `docker-unsecure-group/eclipse-temurin` | 404 | — | — |

B is what `NexusDetector` builds today, and it is the one form that cannot pull.
D is the same trick as A applied to the group, and it does not work: a group is
reachable only through its own connector.

And A is settled **per repository**, not per instance:

| Proxy | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| `dhi-io-proxy` | 200 | 200 |
| `k8s-io-proxy` | 200 | 200 |
| `docker-io-proxy` | 404 | 200 |
| `quay-io-proxy` | 404 | 200 |

`docker-io-proxy/library/nginx` answering B and not A is the decisive pair: the
image is there and reachable, the path-prefix route is not. Whether a Docker
repository answers on a path prefix, a dedicated connector port or a subdomain is
a setting on **that repository** — `docker.httpPort`, `docker.httpsPort`,
`docker.subdomain`.

#### Why no synthesis can be right

Those three fields live in the repository's detailed configuration, behind
`GET /service/rest/v1/repositories/{format}/{type}/{name}` — which answers **403**
here for an ordinary pull account. The public
`GET /service/rest/v1/repositories/{name}` returns the summary shape,
`"attributes": {}`, carrying neither `memberNames` nor the connector fields.

So the one endpoint that would say what the members are is also the one that would
say how to reach them, and an instance that refuses it refuses both. That settles
the question the same way §3.8 decision F settled `provider`: **the addressing is
declared, not sniffed.** Guessing is what D39 already is.

#### The design — one field

`repo_prefix`, on `config.RegistryItem` and on `cache.RegistryGroupMember`. The
four connector modes collapse onto the pair `(url, repo_prefix)`:

| Mode | `url` | `repo_prefix` |
|---|---|---|
| path-based routing | `pic-nexus.spw.dev.wallonie.be` | `dhi-io-proxy` |
| HTTP/HTTPS connector | `pic-nexus.spw.dev.wallonie.be:8082` | — |
| subdomain routing | `dhi-io-proxy.spw.dev.wallonie.be` | — |
| group connector (form C) | `pic-nexus-docker-unsecure-group.spw…` | — |

Both directions derive from that one pair, which is the whole point: the prefix
goes in front of the repository name, the host stays `url`, and browse and pull
cannot disagree about which repository they mean — the disagreement being exactly
what D39 is.

Apply it **once**, in `submitSearch`, where the entry is in hand. The prefix is
then already part of `MultiRegistryTag.Repo`, so `multiImageName` needs no change
and neither does `registryAPIURL`. Teaching both of them about the prefix would
be two places free to drift — the same argument that gave the configuration view
one pointer accessor instead of a get/set pair.

#### What it unlocks

The request this came from: **one checkbox per proxy**. Declare a proxy per line
(`kind: registry`, `url: <host>`, `repo_prefix: dhi-io-proxy`) and the picker
built in §3.8 already does the rest. No discovery in the critical path — which
matters precisely because discovery is what is 403 here.

That is what **D40** had to be fixed for: those entries all share one host, and
until the picker keyed its selection on the entry rather than on the URL, one
per proxy meant one checkbox for all of them. It is fixed, so this no longer
waits on anything.

#### Scope

| Site | Change |
|---|---|
| `config.RegistryItem` | `repo_prefix` field; absent in an existing config and that stays valid |
| `config/registries.go` | validate at load: no leading or trailing `/`, refused on `kind: group` |
| `registrymgr.GroupMember` | carry a prefix instead of a synthesised URL |
| `NexusDetector` | emit `(host, prefix)`; leave the prefix empty when it cannot know |
| `cache.RegistryGroupMember` | carry it, so a discovered member can too |
| `RegistryForm` | one text field, shown for `kind: registry` |
| `submitSearch` | prepend the prefix to the repo, once |
| `entryFor` | resolve a result by entry key, not by URL — every member of a host answers to the same URL once the prefix carries the difference, so a result becomes unattributable (the one site D40 deliberately left alone) |
| `memberKey` | follow whatever tells two members apart once it is no longer the URL |
| Registries tab | show it — an entry whose URL is a bare host says nothing on its own |

Deliberately not done:

- **No probing to pick the form.** Trying A, then B, then a connector port is
  several requests per member per search to answer what the config can state, and
  it would make a member's address depend on which probe answered first.
- **No prefix on a group.** Form D is 404. A group's address is its connector,
  and that is its `url`.
- **No attempt to make `NexusDetector` fill the prefix in** where the detailed
  endpoint is refused. An empty prefix against a bare host is wrong and visibly
  so; a synthesised `/repository/` URL is wrong and plausible, which is D39.

#### Tests worth writing first

- A member with a prefix browses `<host>/v2/<prefix>/<repo>/tags/list` **and**
  pulls `<host>/<prefix>/<repo>:<tag>` — the pair D39 fails, so it fails on the
  current code.
- A member with no prefix produces byte-identical requests to today.
- A `repo_prefix` on a `kind: group` entry fails `LoadContext` rather than loading.

**80.7 % overall — the agreed 80 % target is met.**

| Phase | Scope | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `internal/ui/testutil` Bubble Tea harness | **done** (100 %) |

The project's own coding rules cap files at 800 lines. **None now exceeds it.**

all, and pulling it out of a 2000-line file is what made it obvious it deserved
tests of its own.

`internal/ui/netdiag/model.go` (1114 lines) was split into `validation.go`,
### The race detector sees only what the tests run

**It runs locally now.** `mise run test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C
compiler on `PATH`; without one it fails with `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found`,
which is what this entry used to be about. The Windows development machine has
one — `gcc 16.1.0` (MinGW-w64, `x86_64-posix-seh`), with `go env CGO_ENABLED`
reading `1` and `CC` reading `gcc` — so the check is available before a push
rather than only after one.

Measured on 2026-08-14 with `go test -race -count=1 ./...`, so nothing came from
the test cache: **no data race, across all 29 packages that have tests** (three
have none). It costs two to three minutes wall-clock, and two packages are most
of it — `internal/ui/oci_resources` at 47 s and `internal/scan` at 33 s.

**CI still runs it, and that is not redundant.** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs
`mise run test-race` on every push and pull request on `ubuntu-latest`. A race is
a scheduling accident, so a second machine with a different core count and a
different scheduler is a second sample rather than a repeat of the first — and
CI is what covers a contributor whose machine has no toolchain.

What has not changed is the limit worth keeping in mind: **the detector only
sees code the tests actually execute**, and coverage is 80.7 %. Rule 110
violations in untested paths remain invisible whichever machine runs it. The two
efforts compound, so this stays an argument for the coverage phases rather than a
substitute for them.

`internal/scan` is the package it has most to say about, since `Scanner.Scan` is
the only place in the application that fans out to concurrent goroutines writing
one shared result. Its tests drive all five stages at once, so that fan-out is
under the detector — and now under it locally, where a `Cmd` is being changed,
rather than only where the change is being reported on.

1	// Package datatable is the shared mechanism behind the application's tables.
2	//
3	// What was shared before was only the *look* — theme.DefaultTableStyles,
4	// TableStylesForState/ForSeverity, components.FilterBar, theme.TimeAgo. Column
5	// widths, sorting, sort arrows, filter matching, cursor clamping and
6	// cursor-to-object resolution were written out again in each of the fifteen
7	// tables, and drifted:
8	//
9	//   - Rule 116's width invariant is broken by five of the twelve copies, which
10	//     clamp per column after the remainder has been computed (see widths.go).
11	//   - Two of eight clamp the cursor when the row count shrinks; the rest leave
12	//     it dangling, and oci_resources compensates by jumping to the top on every
13	//     filter toggle, throwing away the scroll position.
14	//   - Nine getSelectedX() replay filter-then-sort by hand to map a cursor back
15	//     to an object, with nothing tying that ordering to the one the rows were
16	//     built from. If they drift, the action lands on the wrong object and says
17	//     nothing. That is the duplication worth removing on correctness grounds.
18	//
19	// Here the filtered, sorted slice is built once and kept, so Selected() cannot
20	// disagree with what is on screen, and Cell func(T) string gives styled text
21	// nowhere to go — Rule 122 by construction rather than by review.

37	// Column describes one column and how to get its value out of an item.
38	type Column[T any] struct {
39		Title string
40		// MinWidth is what the column asks for. It is a request, not a guarantee:
41		// when the terminal is too narrow for every request, the shortfall is
42		// shared out rather than each column defending its own floor.
43		MinWidth int
44		// Flex is the column's share of the space left over. 0 keeps it at
45		// MinWidth; the leftover is split between the flexible ones by weight.
46		Flex int
47		// Cell returns the text for this column. Plain text only: it is measured
48		// and truncated before anything is applied to it, and runewidth counts an
49		// escape sequence's bytes as width — a styled string is cut mid-escape and
50		// bleeds over every row below it (Rule 122). Taking a string rather than a
51		// styled value is what makes that unexpressible here.
52		Cell func(T) string
53		// Style colours the cell after it has been measured and truncated, which is
54		// the only order in which colour is safe (see render.go). Nil leaves the
55		// cell in the table's own colours.
56		//
57		// It is not consulted for the selected row: that row is handed to
58		// styles.Selected whole, and a colour inside it would end the highlight
59		// mid-row. A column cannot ask for that back.
60		Style func(T) lipgloss.Style
61		// Less sorts by this column. Nil means the column cannot be sorted by, and
62		// `.` skips it.
63		Less func(a, b T) bool
64		// Search is what the text filter matches against. Nil means the column does
65		// not participate.
66		Search func(T) string
67	}

117	// New builds a table from its configuration.
118	func New[T any](cfg Config[T]) Model[T] {
119		cols := make([]table.Column, len(cfg.Columns))
120		for i, c := range cfg.Columns {
121			cols[i] = table.Column{Title: c.Title, Width: c.MinWidth}
122		}
123		t := table.New(table.WithColumns(cols), table.WithFocused(true), table.WithHeight(10))
124	
125		bar := components.NewFilterBar()
126		if len(cfg.Tokens) > 0 {
127			bar = components.NewFilterBarWithTokens(cfg.Tokens)
128		}
129	
130		m := Model[T]{cfg: cfg, table: t, bar: bar, sortColumn: cfg.SortColumn, sortDesc: cfg.SortDesc}
131		// Through setStyles rather than the table alone: a table rendered before
132		// anything calls applyStyles — one built and drawn in the same frame — would
133		// otherwise render with the zero Styles, which carries no cell padding and
134		// so lays out two cells narrower per column than every width was solved for.
135		m.setStyles(theme.DefaultTableStyles())
136		// The invariant the rest of the file rests on: sortColumn is either -1 or a
137		// column that can actually be sorted by. Settling it once here is what lets
138		// CycleSort and sorted() stop re-checking — and what stops `.` getting stuck
139		// flipping the direction of a column with no comparator.
140		if m.sortColumn >= len(cfg.Columns) || (m.sortColumn >= 0 && cfg.Columns[m.sortColumn].Less == nil) {
141			m.sortColumn = -1
142			// A direction with no column to apply it to would put the header arrow
143			// on nothing and make `.` open on descending.
144			m.sortDesc = false
145		}
146		return m
147	}

149	// SetItems replaces the contents. Filtering, sorting, row building and the
150	// cursor clamp all happen here and only here, which is what stops a cursor from
151	// being left pointing past the end — bubbles/table's SetRows does not clamp, and
152	// the stale cursor is invisible until the user presses a key.
153	func (m *Model[T]) SetItems(items []T) {
154		m.items = items

164	// Selected returns the item under the cursor. The bool is false when there is
165	// nothing to select, which is the only case a caller has to handle.
166	func (m *Model[T]) Selected() (T, bool) {
167		cursor := m.table.Cursor()
168		if cursor < 0 || cursor >= len(m.visible) {
169			var zero T
170			return zero, false
171		}
172		return m.visible[cursor], true

239	// Resize recomputes the column widths for a viewport of this width (Rule 116).
240	// The width passed is the full viewport width, borders included; the borders and
241	// the per-cell padding are subtracted here so no caller has to remember to.
242	func (m *Model[T]) Resize(width, height int) {
243		m.width = width
244		widths := solveWidths(m.cfg.Columns, availableFor(width, len(m.cfg.Columns)))
245	
246		cols := m.table.Columns()
247		for i := range cols {
248			cols[i].Width = widths[i]
249			cols[i].Title = m.titleFor(i)
250		}
251		m.table.SetColumns(cols)
252		m.bar.Resize(width)
253		if height > 0 {
254			m.SetHeight(height)
255		}
256		m.afterCursorMove() // the selected row is pinned to this width

259	// The sort arrows, and what they cost. Named because widths.go has to reserve
260	// room for them: a column's MinWidth is the view's statement about its content,
261	// and it knows nothing about two cells this package appends to the header.
262	const (
263		sortArrowAsc  = " ▲"
264		sortArrowDesc = " ▼"
265	)

267	// titleFor returns a column's header, with a sort arrow on the active one.
268	func (m *Model[T]) titleFor(i int) string {
269		if i != m.sortColumn {
270			return m.cfg.Columns[i].Title
271		}
272		if m.sortDesc {
273			return m.cfg.Columns[i].Title + sortArrowDesc
274		}
275		return m.cfg.Columns[i].Title + sortArrowAsc

278	// CycleSort advances the sort: ascending, descending, then on to the next
279	// sortable column (Rule 111's `.`). Returns to no sort after the last one when
280	// the table opened unsorted, so the original order stays reachable.
281	func (m *Model[T]) CycleSort() {
282		sortable := m.sortableColumns()
283		if len(sortable) == 0 {
284			return
285		}
286		switch {
287		case m.sortColumn < 0:
288			m.sortColumn, m.sortDesc = sortable[0], false
289		case !m.sortDesc:
290			m.sortDesc = true
291		default:
292			m.sortColumn, m.sortDesc = m.nextSortable(sortable), false
293		}
294		m.rebuild()
295		m.Resize(m.width, 0) // the arrow moved
296	}
297	
298	// nextSortable returns the column after the current one, wrapping to the first —
299	// or to -1 when the table opened unsorted, so "no sort" is a stop on the cycle.
300	//
301	// slices.Index rather than a loop with a trailing fallback: the current column
302	// is always in sortable (New guarantees it), and a fallback that cannot run is
303	// a branch nothing can ever check.
304	func (m *Model[T]) nextSortable(sortable []int) int {
305		if at := slices.Index(sortable, m.sortColumn); at+1 < len(sortable) {
306			return sortable[at+1]
307		}
308		if m.cfg.SortColumn < 0 {
309			return -1
310		}
311		return sortable[0]
312	}

314	func (m *Model[T]) sortableColumns() []int {
315		var out []int
316		for i, c := range m.cfg.Columns {
317			if c.Less != nil {
318				out = append(out, i)
319			}
320		}
321		return out
322	}

324	// SortState reports the column sorted by and its direction, for tests and for
325	// views that show it elsewhere. Column is -1 when nothing is sorted.
326	func (m *Model[T]) SortState() (column int, desc bool) { return m.sortColumn, m.sortDesc }

328	// Update handles the keys every table shares: navigation, `/` for the search,
329	// `.` for the sort, and whatever the filter bar takes while it is focused.
330	// Anything else is left alone, so the view keeps its own actions.
331	func (m *Model[T]) Update(msg tea.Msg) tea.Cmd {
332		if m.bar.InEditMode() {
333			var cmd tea.Cmd
334			m.bar, cmd = m.bar.Update(msg)
335			m.rebuild()
336			return cmd
337		}
338	
339		key, ok := msg.(tea.KeyMsg)
340		if !ok {
341			return nil
342		}
343		switch key.String() {
344		case "/":
345			// A table with nothing to search does not claim the key: activating a
346			// search that can only ever match nothing would empty the list, and the
347			// bar the user needs to see why is not in that view's footer.
348			if !m.Searchable() {
349				return nil
350			}
351			return m.bar.ActivateSearch()
352		case ".":
353			m.CycleSort()
354		case "up", "k":
355			m.table.MoveUp(1)
356			m.afterCursorMove()
357		case "down", "j":
358			m.table.MoveDown(1)
359			m.afterCursorMove()
360		case "pgup":
361			m.table.MoveUp(m.table.Height())
362			m.afterCursorMove()
363		case "pgdown":
364			m.table.MoveDown(m.table.Height())
365			m.afterCursorMove()
366		case "g", "home":
367			m.table.GotoTop()
368			m.afterCursorMove()
369		case "G", "end":
370			m.table.GotoBottom()
371			m.afterCursorMove()
372		}
373		return nil
374	}

376	// SetTokenActive toggles one of the bar's filter tokens and re-applies it.
377	func (m *Model[T]) SetTokenActive(label string, active bool) {
378		m.bar.SetTokenActive(label, active)
379		m.rebuild()
380	}

382	// IsTokenActive reports whether a toggle filter is on.
383	func (m *Model[T]) IsTokenActive(label string) bool { return m.bar.IsTokenActive(label) }
384	
385	// rebuild filters, sorts, writes the rows and puts the cursor somewhere real.
386	func (m *Model[T]) rebuild() {
387		m.visible = m.sorted(m.filtered())
388	
389		rows := make([]table.Row, len(m.visible))
390		for i, item := range m.visible {
391			cells := make(table.Row, len(m.cfg.Columns))
392			for j, c := range m.cfg.Columns {
393				cells[j] = c.Cell(item)
394			}
395			rows[i] = cells
396		}
397		m.table.SetRows(rows)
398	
399		// bubbles/table leaves the cursor where it was, so a list that just got
400		// shorter strands it past the end until the user presses a key. It also
401		// reports -1 while there are no rows at all, and that has to be taken back
402		// when rows return — a filter typed past its last match and then corrected
403		// would otherwise leave the table showing rows none of which is selected.
404		switch cursor := m.table.Cursor(); {
405		case len(rows) == 0:
406			// -1 is bubbles' own "nothing selected", and what it reports for a
407			// table that never had rows. Leaving the old index would make an empty
408			// list the one state where the cursor points past the end.
409			m.table.SetCursor(-1)
410		case cursor >= len(rows):
411			m.table.SetCursor(len(rows) - 1)
412		case cursor < 0:
413			m.table.SetCursor(0)
414		}
415		m.afterCursorMove()
416	}
417	
418	// afterCursorMove is what every cursor, height and item change ends with: the
419	// styles follow the selected item, and the scroll window follows the cursor.
420	// Keeping them on one call is what stops a new call site from remembering one
421	// and forgetting the other — the offset was invisible while bubbles owned it.
422	func (m *Model[T]) afterCursorMove() {
423		m.clampOffset()
424		m.applyStyles()
425	}

427	// applyStyles asks the view for the styles that go with the selected item.
428	func (m *Model[T]) applyStyles() {
429		if !m.table.Focused() {
430			return // Blur owns the styles until Focus takes them back
431		}
432		styles := theme.DefaultTableStyles()
433		if item, ok := m.Selected(); ok && m.cfg.SelectedStyles != nil {
434			styles = m.cfg.SelectedStyles(item)
435		}
436		// Pin the selected row to the full content width. Column widths are counted
437		// in cells, and a Nerd Font icon does not always render as wide as it
438		// counts, so the highlight otherwise stops short of the right border by
439		// however much the row's icons disagreed. Padding to a width the row can
440		// never exceed is a no-op when they agree.
441		if m.width > 2 {
442			styles.Selected = styles.Selected.Width(m.width - 2)
443		}
444		m.setStyles(styles)
445	}
446	
447	// setStyles keeps bubbles' copy and this package's in step. The rendering reads
448	// the one here (render.go); bubbles' is still what Table() reports, which the
449	// tests and any view reaching for the raw table expect to be current.
450	func (m *Model[T]) setStyles(styles table.Styles) {
451		m.styles = styles
452		m.table.SetStyles(styles)
453	}

455	// filtered applies the search query and the toggle filters.
456	func (m *Model[T]) filtered() []T {
457		query := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(m.bar.SearchQuery()))
458		active := m.activeTokens()
459	
460		out := make([]T, 0, len(m.items))
461		for _, item := range m.items {
462			if m.cfg.TokenMatch != nil && !m.cfg.TokenMatch(item, active) {
463				continue
464			}
465			if query != "" && !m.matchesQuery(item, query) {
466				continue
467			}
468			out = append(out, item)
469		}
470		return out
471	}
472	
473	func (m *Model[T]) activeTokens() map[string]bool {
474		active := make(map[string]bool, len(m.cfg.Tokens))
475		for _, tok := range m.cfg.Tokens {
476			if m.bar.IsTokenActive(tok.Label) {
477				active[tok.Label] = true
478			}
479		}
480		return active
481	}
482	
483	// matchesQuery tests the query against each searchable column and then against
484	// the row as a whole.
485	//
486	// The row-level pass is what keeps a query spanning two fields — "tcp 22" over a
487	// ports list — working: netdiag matched against a joined haystack while the
488	// other four filter loops matched per field, and per field alone would have
489	// quietly dropped those matches on migration. Matching both ways is a superset
490	// of either, so no view loses anything and they all gain the same thing.
491	func (m *Model[T]) matchesQuery(item T, query string) bool {
492		var joined strings.Builder
493		for _, c := range m.cfg.Columns {
494			if c.Search == nil {
495				continue
496			}
497			value := c.Search(item)
498			if strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(value), query) {
499				return true
500			}
501			if joined.Len() > 0 {
502				joined.WriteByte(' ')
503			}
504			joined.WriteString(value)
505		}
506		return strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(joined.String()), query)
507	}
508	
509	// sorted orders the visible slice. SliceStable, because sort.Slice is not and
510	// two rows equal on the sort column would otherwise swap between rebuilds.
511	func (m *Model[T]) sorted(items []T) []T {
512		if m.sortColumn < 0 {
513			return items
514		}
515		less := m.cfg.Columns[m.sortColumn].Less // never nil — see New
516		desc := m.sortDesc
517		sort.SliceStable(items, func(i, j int) bool {
518			if desc {
519				return less(items[j], items[i])
520			}
521			return less(items[i], items[j])
522		})
523		return items
524	}

187	// the list, not to any repository: one spinner, on every row that is running.

29		URL   string

32		// for a member. It is what the result filter resolves labels through, and
33		// what replaced matching on URL — two registries configured with the same

208	// buildEntries expands every configured registry into the lines the picker
209	// shows: a group into its cached members under a header, anything else into
210	// itself.
211	//
212	// A selection is remembered as the entries that were *un*checked, so a member
213	// discovered since the last visit arrives checked like every other new one.
214	func (b *RegistryBrowser) buildEntries(groups map[string]cache.RegistryGroupEntry, deselected map[string]bool) {
215		b.entries = nil
216		b.rows = nil
217		for _, reg := range b.registries {
218			alias := browserAlias(reg)
219			// Members share their group's host and therefore its single credential
220			// entry, so they share the decision the group made about using it.
221			mode := config.ResolveAuthMode(reg, nil)
222	
223			members := groups[reg.Slug].Members
224			if reg.Kind != config.KindGroup || len(members) == 0 {
225				// A group nobody has discovered yet is offered as itself: it is a
226				// pullable registry too, and hiding it would be worse than listing
227				// it without the members it may have.
228				b.rows = append(b.rows, pickerRow{label: alias, entry: len(b.entries)})

230					URL: reg.URL, Alias: alias, Slug: reg.Slug, authMode: mode,
231					key: reg.Slug,
232				})
233				continue
234			}
235	
236			b.rows = append(b.rows, pickerRow{groupSlug: reg.Slug, label: alias, entry: -1})

238				b.rows = append(b.rows, pickerRow{label: "  " + m.Alias, entry: len(b.entries)})

240					URL:         m.URL,

242					Slug:        reg.Slug,
243					ParentAlias: alias,
244					ParentSlug:  reg.Slug,
245					parentURL:   reg.URL,
246					authMode:    mode,

3	import "github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss"
4	
5	// Rule 116: the column widths must sum to exactly the space available, or the
6	// selected row stops short of the right viewport border.
7	//
8	// Every view enforced that the same way — last column absorbs the remainder —
9	// and several then applied a per-column `max(…, floor)` *after* the remainder
10	// was computed, which silently pushes the sum back over. `workspaces` overflows
11	// by 34 columns on a 120-wide terminal that way.
12	//
13	// The fix is not a better clamp. It is to distribute the shortfall across the
14	// columns instead of letting each one defend its own floor: a floor that cannot
15	// be honoured has to be given up by somebody, and deciding that here is what
16	// makes the invariant hold at every width rather than most of them.
17	
18	// borderWidth is the viewport's two vertical borders.
19	const borderWidth = 2
20	
21	// cellPadding is what bubbles/table adds per column — Padding(0, 1).
22	const cellPadding = 2
23	
24	// availableFor returns the width the columns have to share, given the full
25	// viewport width. Negative when the terminal cannot even hold the borders and
26	// the padding, which the solver reads as "no room at all".
27	func availableFor(viewportWidth, numColumns int) int {
28		return viewportWidth - borderWidth - numColumns*cellPadding
29	}
30	
31	// sortArrowWidth is what titleFor appends to the sorted column's header.
32	// Measured rather than assumed: the arrows are not ASCII, and bubbles/table
33	// truncates the header with the same rune widths lipgloss counts.
34	var sortArrowWidth = max(lipgloss.Width(sortArrowAsc), lipgloss.Width(sortArrowDesc))
35	
36	// askFor is the width a column needs, which is not always the MinWidth it
37	// states.
38	//
39	// MinWidth is the view's statement about the column's *content*. A sortable
40	// column also carries a header this package widens by an arrow, and nothing
41	// told the view about those two cells — so a count column asking for 5 rendered
42	// "CRIT ▼" into it and lost exactly the character that says how it is sorted.
43	//
44	// The room is reserved for every sortable column, not only the one currently
45	// sorted: reserving it on demand would resize the column each time `.` moved
46	// the sort, shifting every column beside it.
47	func askFor[T any](c Column[T]) int {
48		width := max(c.MinWidth, 0)
49		if c.Less == nil {
50			return width
51		}
52		return max(width, lipgloss.Width(c.Title)+sortArrowWidth)
53	}
54	
55	// solveWidths distributes available across the columns.
56	//
57	// Fixed columns (Flex == 0) ask for MinWidth. Flexible ones ask for MinWidth
58	// and share whatever is left in proportion to their Flex weight. When there is
59	// not enough for everyone, the shortfall comes out of the flexible columns
60	// first and the fixed ones only after — a fixed column is fixed because its
61	// content has a known size, so it is the last thing worth truncating.
62	//
63	// The result always sums to exactly max(available, 0).
64	func solveWidths[T any](columns []Column[T], available int) []int {
65		widths := make([]int, len(columns))
66		if len(columns) == 0 || available <= 0 {
67			return widths
68		}
69	
70		total := 0
71		for i, c := range columns {
72			widths[i] = askFor(c)
73			total += widths[i]
74		}
75	
76		switch {
77		case total < available:
78			grow(columns, widths, available-total)
79		case total > available:
80			shrink(columns, widths, total-available)
81		}
82		return widths
83	}
84	
85	// grow hands the surplus to the flexible columns by weight, giving the last one
86	// the rounding remainder so the sum is exact. With no flexible column the last
87	// column absorbs it, which is what every view did by hand.
88	func grow[T any](columns []Column[T], widths []int, surplus int) {
89		weight := 0
90		last := -1
91		for i, c := range columns {
92			if c.Flex > 0 {
93				weight += c.Flex
94				last = i
95			}
96		}
97		if weight == 0 {
98			widths[len(widths)-1] += surplus
99			return
100		}
101	
102		given := 0
103		for i, c := range columns {
104			if c.Flex <= 0 || i == last {
105				continue
106			}
107			share := surplus * c.Flex / weight
108			widths[i] += share
109			given += share
110		}
111		widths[last] += surplus - given
112	}
113

Registries, the registry browser's tags, network-inspect and netdiag's results).
A new table uses it; there is no second way to build one, and `bubbles/table` is
imported outside this package only for its `Styles` type.

The Registries tab is the one worth knowing about, because it shows **two
populations in one table** — the configured entries, and one group's discovered
members after `→`. `datatable.Model[T]` is generic over a single `T`, so
`registryRow` carries both and holds the index of the config entry it stands
for, `-1` for a member. That index is what `getSelectedRegistry` resolves
through: indexing `m.registries` by row number is right only while the table
neither sorts nor filters, which is exactly the dependency nothing signalled.
`explorerRow` exists for the same reason.

Three views keep a filter of their own, and deliberately. `security` selects
findings by tab and by severity, and `status` drives both its tables from one
search box so the header counts agree — in both cases the view filters and calls
`SetItems`, because a `FilterBar` query narrows a list that is already settled
and these decide which rows exist at all. `security` also calls `GotoTop`
explicitly on a tab change, which is the reset `SetItems` does not make. The
registry browser is the third: its text filter and its registry filter narrow
the tags *before* the table sees them, and its bar is drawn in the OCI view's
own footer rather than the table's. Its **sort** is the table's — `.` cycles
Tag and Updated through `CycleSort`, and `SetSort` is what puts a new search
back on the default order.

#### Ce que ça a donné

Les quatre sont migrées et il ne reste **aucune `bubbles/table`** dans
l'application : le paquet n'est plus importé ailleurs que pour son type
`Styles`.

La contrainte « uniquement la couleur du texte » a tenu, à une chose près qui
n'est pas une régression : la table des tags **avait déjà** un tri, et il est
passé à `CycleSort`. Le cycle est identique — Tag ↑, Tag ↓, Updated ↑,
Updated ↓, retour — parce que `datatable` cycle exactement les colonnes qui
portent un `Less`, et il n'y en a que ces deux. Les flèches d'en-tête, écrites
à la main dans `rebuildTagTable`, tombent avec. Une seule chose manquait pour
que ce soit un remplacement exact : **`datatable.SetSort`**, le pendant écrivain
de `SortState` — `submitSearch` remet l'ordre par défaut au début d'une nouvelle
recherche, et faire le tour du cycle avec `CycleSort` n'est pas ça.

Le filtre texte de la table des tags, lui, **reste dans la vue** : il réduit les
tags *avant* que la table les voie, comme le filtre par registre à côté de lui,
et sa barre est rendue dans le footer de la vue OCI, pas dans celle de la table.
C'est le cas `security` / `status` déjà documenté.

**Registres : `registryRow` porte l'indice de l'entrée de config**, `-1` pour un
membre découvert. C'était prévu comme la seule difficulté de forme, et ça a payé
tout de suite : `getSelectedRegistry` indexait `m.registries` par numéro de
ligne, ce qui n'est juste que tant que la table ne trie ni ne filtre.

**Trois défauts trouvés en migrant**, chacun avec un test vérifié contre
l'ancien code :

- **D41**, ci-dessus (§1.1) : URL clampée après le reste, deux colonnes
  négatives sous 80 colonnes.
- **network-inspect soustrayait les bordures deux fois** — la vue lui passe déjà
  la largeur de contenu — donc ses colonnes totalisaient deux cellules de moins
  que la place disponible, à *toutes* les largeurs, et la ligne sélectionnée
  s'arrêtait avant la bordure droite.
- **netdiag débordait sous 62 colonnes** : le plancher `max(width-2, 30)` faisait
  résoudre les largeurs pour un viewport plus large que le vrai.

Le spinner « refreshing » de la colonne Members passe au *frame* brut plutôt
qu'à `spinner.View()` : c'était la Rule 122 latente que §3.21 nommait, et un
test l'interdit maintenant.

Enfin, la table de résultats netdiag **garde son curseur** : elle était
reconstruite par `table.New` à chaque mise à jour, donc un résultat tardif
ramenait la ligne sous le curseur de l'utilisateur en haut.

J'ai regardé comment c'est câblé aujourd'hui. Le trou est réel et je peux le situer précisément.

`handleConfirmYes` (`results.go:17`) déclenche la `Cmd` et retourne **sans toucher au modèle** — aucun marqueur, aucun message footer. La ligne reste identique jusqu'à ce que `ImageActionMsg` revienne et relance `fetchImages()`. Même chose dans containers pour stop/restart/pause/remove.

Le pire cas n'est pas `docker rmi` mais **`docker stop`** : `internal/docker/containers.go:150` appelle `docker stop` sans `-t`, donc SIGTERM puis SIGKILL après le délai de grâce — **10 secondes** pendant lesquelles rien ne bouge à l'écran. C'est exactement le symptôme que §3.16 décrit pour la modale « Pulling... » : indiscernable d'un gel.

## Faut-il bloquer le déplacement ? Non — mais il faut bloquer autre chose

C'est la partie où je suis net, et le code tranche déjà :

**Le curseur ne doit pas être verrouillé.** Trois raisons, dans l'ordre de force :

1. **Le projet a déjà décidé le contraire.** Un scan tourne avec un spinner dans la cellule et l'utilisateur continue de naviguer — c'est toute la raison d'être de `imageRow.Scanning`. Idem pour `membersCell`'s `refreshing` et le sync de workspaces. Verrouiller ici créerait une deuxième règle pour la même situation.
2. **L'action ne dépend déjà plus du curseur.** `removeImageCmd(img.ID, name)` a capturé l'ID au moment du `enter`. Une fois partie, la position du curseur ne peut plus rien changer — le verrou protégerait contre un risque qui n'existe pas.
3. **Un curseur qui ne répond pas, c'est le symptôme qu'on essaie de soigner.** L'utilisateur ne sait pas si c'est « occupé » ou « planté ».

**Ce qu'il faut bloquer, c'est l'objet, pas le curseur** — la règle `busy(path)` de workspaces (`sync.go:38`). Aujourd'hui rien n'empêche de confirmer deux fois une suppression lente et de lancer deux `docker rmi`. Le second échoue avec « No such image », et l'utilisateur voit `Action failed — check logs` sur une suppression qui a réussi. C'est le vrai défaut latent ici, et il est indépendant de l'indicateur.

## Trois options pour l'indicateur

| | Ce que c'est | Coût |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Spinner dans une cellule existante** | La cellule « qu'est-ce que fait cette ligne » de chaque vue prend un mot de plus : containers → l'icône d'état (`⠸ stopping`), images → `Scanned`, registries → `Members` | **Un type de ligne par vue.** `containers`, `networks` et `volumes` sont des `datatable.Model[docker.Container]` etc. — des objets du domaine. Il faut leur inventer un `containerRow`, comme la migration vient de le faire pour registries et tags |
| **B. Décoration au niveau de la ligne, dans `datatable`** | `Config.Busy func(T) string` : `""` = ligne normale, sinon le libellé. Le renderer grise la ligne et pose le libellé | Une API en plus, mais **une seule implémentation et un seul rendu** pour les quinze tables |
| **C. Suppression optimiste** | La ligne disparaît tout de suite, revient si ça échoue | Aucun spinner — mais `docker rmi` échoue souvent (image utilisée par un conteneur), donc on ment une fois sur trois. **À écarter** |

**Je recommande A d'abord, B seulement si ça se répand.** Raisonnement : `datatable` ne sait rien du domaine aujourd'hui, et l'option B lui apprendrait qu'une ligne peut être « en train de faire quelque chose » — c'est une notion métier. Le YAGNI de tes propres règles s'applique : deux vues suffisent à valider la forme, et si les six finissent par en avoir besoin, la remontée dans `datatable` sera mécanique parce que le patron `imageRow` sera déjà partout.

Le seul argument sérieux pour B tout de suite, c'est que **A coûte trois types de ligne d'un coup** (containers, networks, volumes) — c'est le même travail que §3.21 vient de faire, donc ni surprenant ni risqué, mais ce n'est pas gratuit.

## Ce que je ferais concrètement

1. `m.pendingActions map[string]string` (clé de l'objet → verbe), posé dans `handleConfirmYes`, effacé dans `handleImageAction` / `handleContainerAction`.
2. Un garde-fou `busy(key)` sur le chemin de confirmation, avec le message footer déjà normalisé par la Rule 128.
3. Le libellé dans la cellule d'état, en **texte brut avec le frame du spinner** — `spinner.Dot.Frames[...]`, jamais `spinner.View()` (Rule 122, c'est exactement le piège que la migration vient de retirer de `membersCell`).
4. La ligne occupée en `DimStyle` : elle décrit un état qui est en train de cesser d'être vrai.

**Un cas ne rentre pas dans ce cadre et mérite d'être traité à part : `prune`.** Il n'agit sur aucune ligne — il agit sur la table entière. Y coller le même mécanisme obligerait à marquer toutes les lignes, ce qui dirait faux (prune n'en supprime que certaines). Là, l'indicateur est au niveau de la table, et le patron existe déjà : la ligne de footer rendue depuis l'état de l'opération, comme `syncStatusLine` de §3.17 — pas `footerInfo`, dont le timer de 3 s expirerait au milieu.

Si tu veux, je peux l'implémenter sur containers en premier : c'est là que le gel de 10 s se voit, et ça sert de banc d'essai avant de décider si ça remonte dans `datatable`.

Je souhaite partir sur B, ce doit être une fonctionnalité générique d'un datatable. J'aurais envie d'avoir une colonne en première position qui pourrait prendre une icone de statut de ligne. Cette colonne pourrait contenir le statut d'un container avec les différentes icone par statut, mais si une action de transition est en cours alors il y a une icone genre spinner ou engrenage qui dit que quelque chose se passe. D'accord sur le principe, et la colonne en position 0 paye **avant même** le spinner : aujourd'hui l'état du conteneur est collé à la cellule Image (`stateIcon(c.State) + " " + c.Image`), ce qui oblige la colonne Image à déclarer `Search: c.Image + " " + c.State` pour compenser le fait que l'icône n'est pas là où elle devrait être. La sortir remet chaque colonne sur son sujet, et `stateIcon` a déjà tout le vocabulaire (`running`, `paused`, `exited`, `created`/`restarting`, `dead`).

Trois choses sur lesquelles je ne partirais pas tel quel.

## Une seule colonne, mais pas une seule fonction

« Ce que l'objet **est** » et « ce qui lui **arrive** » n'ont ni la même durée de vie ni la même source de vérité : l'état vient de docker au prochain refresh, la transition est une connaissance propre à DevDesk. Les fusionner dans le **glyphe** est juste — c'est ton idée et elle est bonne. Les fusionner dans l'**API** ferait ré-implémenter la règle de préséance dans chaque vue, c'est-à-dire exactement la duplication que `datatable` existe pour supprimer.

Donc : la vue déclare une colonne de statut ordinaire, et **`datatable` écrase sa cellule quand la ligne est occupée**. Pas de nouveau type de colonne, juste un override. « Occupé gagne sur l'état » est écrit une fois.

## L'obstacle réel : les colonnes ne ferment sur rien

C'est un invariant énoncé du paquet — « les colonnes sont construites une fois, dans `New`, donc leurs `Cell` ne peuvent pas remonter dans le modèle ». C'est la raison d'être de `imageRow`. Un `Busy func(T) string` posé sur la `Config` tomberait droit dedans : il devrait fermer sur la map des actions en cours du modèle.

La sortie qui marche est de séparer l'identité de l'état :

```go
datatable.Config[T]{
    Key: func(c docker.Container) string { return c.ID },  // nil = facilité désactivée
    StatusColumn: 0,
}

m.table.SetBusy(map[string]string{id: "stopping"})  // depuis Update, Rule 110
m.table.AdvanceSpinner()                            // depuis le tick spinner existant
m.table.IsBusy(id)                                  // le garde-fou, gratuit
```

`IsBusy` est le bonus qui compte : il répond **avant que la ligne existe**, donc c'est lui qui bloque l'objet au moment de la confirmation — le verrou dont on a parlé, celui qui empêche deux `docker rmi` concurrents. Une clé plutôt qu'un drapeau sur la ligne, aussi, parce qu'un refresh périodique remplace les lignes pendant l'action : une map par identité survit sans que la vue ait à penser à recalculer la décoration.

Le spinner : `datatable` ne peut pas tenir un `spinner.Model` — il lui faut un `Cmd`, donc un tick, donc la vue (Rule 110). **La frame vit dans la table, le tick reste dans la vue.**

Et sur gear vs spinner : **spinner**, sans hésiter. Un engrenage immobile ne distingue pas « ça travaille » de « c'est planté », ce qui est précisément la question à laquelle l'indicateur doit répondre.

## Le style de ligne bute sur la ligne sélectionnée

C'est le piège documenté dans `render.go` : la ligne sous le curseur est passée **entière** à `styles.Selected`, et une couleur à l'intérieur se referme par un reset qui coupe le surlignage au milieu. Donc une ligne occupée *et* sélectionnée ne peut pas être grisée cellule par cellule — il faut passer par `SelectedStyles`.

Comme `datatable` possédera la notion d'occupé, c'est lui qui doit l'appliquer **des deux côtés**, plutôt que de laisser chaque vue y penser. Concrètement : `DimStyle` sur les cellules hors sélection, et le `SelectedStyles` de la vue reçoit l'info pour la ligne sélectionnée.

## Deux réserves à garder en tête

**La largeur.** ~3 cellules sur chaque table qui l'active — donc **opt-in**, jamais automatique, et la colonne **ne doit pas être triable** : `askFor` réserve `width(Title)+2` à une colonne triable, ce que le commentaire de la colonne Secrets qualifie déjà de « cher pour un glyphe ». Titre vide ou un caractère.

**Une ligne qui tourne indéfiniment.** Si l'entrée n'est effacée que sur le message de succès, un échec laisse le spinner à vie — et pire, il masque l'état réel : `docker stop` qui échoue doit revenir à `running`, pas rester sur l'engrenage. Les `Cmd` d'action renvoient toutes un message y compris en erreur, donc la discipline est « effacer sur *toute* issue », avec un test sur le chemin d'erreur. # A row says what it is, and what is happening to it

**§3.22.** `datatable` gains a status column and a notion of a row being busy.
Containers is the first client.

## The problem

`handleConfirmYes` fires the `Cmd` and returns without touching the model
(`oci_resources/results.go:17`, `containers/update.go:463`). Nothing on screen
says an action is running, and `internal/docker/containers.go:150` calls
`docker stop` with no `-t`, so the default ten-second grace period is ten
seconds of a frozen-looking table. That is the symptom §3.16 recorded for the
clone's `"Pulling..."` modal: indistinguishable from a hang.

**The intent was already there and lost its reader.** `containers.Model` has a
`pendingAction` field written in six places, three of them human sentences —
`"Stopping web"`, `"Restarting api"`, `"Pruning containers..."` — and asserted by
four tests. **No rendering code reads it.** The field is overloaded: it also
carries the confirm modal's routing key (`"confirm-delete"`, `"confirm-prune"`),
which `handleConfirmYes` does read. One field, two meanings, and the one nobody
reads is the one that was supposed to be visible.

## The decision behind the shape

Two things share one glyph and must not share one function:

| | What it is | Source of truth | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|---|
| **State** | `running`, `exited`, `paused` | docker, at the next refresh | as long as it is true |
| **Transition** | `stopping`, `removing` | DevDesk itself | one command |

Merging them in the **glyph** is the point — one column answers "what about this
row". Merging them in the **API** would make every table re-implement the
precedence. So `datatable` owns one rule: **busy wins over state**, and it wins
for a reason worth stating — `exited` is precisely what is about to stop being
true.

## Why it cannot be a closure

The package's stated invariant is that columns are built once, in `New`, and
close over nothing; `imageRow` exists because of it. A `Busy func(T) string` on
the `Config` would have to close over the model's map of in-flight actions —
the exact trap the row types avoid.

So identity and state are separated: the config supplies a **`Key func(T) string`**,
and the busy set is held by the table and written from `Update`.

That buys the thing that matters most: **`IsBusy(key)` answers before the row
exists**, so it is also the guard on the confirm path. Today nothing stops a
second `ctrl+d` on a slow removal from firing a second `docker rmi`; the second
fails with "No such image" and the user sees `Action failed` on a removal that
worked.

Keying on identity rather than a flag on the row also survives the periodic
refresh, which replaces the items mid-action.

## API

```go
datatable.Config[T]{
    Key:          func(c docker.Container) string { return c.ID }, // nil ⇒ off
    StatusColumn: 0,                                               // cell the spinner replaces
}

m.table.MarkBusy(id, "Stopping web")   // from Update, Rule 110
m.table.ClearBusy(id)                  // on *every* outcome, error included
m.table.IsBusy(id)                     // the guard
m.table.BusyLabels()                   // sorted, for the footer line
m.table.AdvanceSpinner()               // from the view's existing spinner tick
```

`datatable` cannot hold a `spinner.Model` — a spinner needs a `Cmd`, so a tick,
so the view (Rule 110). **The frame lives in the table, the tick stays in the
view.** A moving spinner rather than a static gear, deliberately: an immobile
glyph cannot tell "working" from "stuck", which is the question being answered.

## Rendering

- The cell at `StatusColumn` renders the spinner frame instead of the column's
  own `Cell`, **whether or not the row is selected** — the glyph is the primary
  signal and has to work everywhere.
- Off the selected row, the busy row's cells go `DimStyle`, the status cell
  `ColorHighlight`. This follows the existing rule that `Style` is not consulted
  for the selected row.
- **On** the selected row the highlight itself changes, because a colour inside
  it would close with a reset and end the highlight mid-row (`render.go`). So
  `theme.TableStylesForState("busy")` — `ColorHighlight` background — overrides
  whatever `SelectedStyles` returned. That is "busy wins over state" again, and
  the colour is not arbitrary: containers already paints docker's own
  transitional states (`created`, `restarting`) in `ColorHighlight`.

## Cost and limits

- The column costs ~3 cells on every table that opts in, so it is **opt-in** and
  **must not be sortable**: `askFor` reserves `width(Title)+2` for a sortable
  column, which the Secrets column already calls expensive for a glyph. Title
  empty or one character.
- A busy entry cleared only on success leaves a row spinning for good — and
  worse, hides the real state. Cleared on **every** outcome, with a test on the
  error path. Same family as §3.11's "a reload keeps an in-flight scan's marker".

## Deliberately out of scope

- **Scans.** Their spinner is in the Scanned column and they do not block the
  object the same way. Folding them in is a separate question.
- **`prune`.** It acts on no row, so marking every row would say something
  false. It belongs to a footer line rendered from the operation's state, like
  `syncStatusLine` (§3.17) — not `footerInfo`, whose three-second timer would
  expire mid-operation.

## Steps

1. `theme.TableStylesForState("busy")`.
2. `datatable`: `Key`, `StatusColumn`, the busy set, `MarkBusy`/`ClearBusy`/
   `IsBusy`/`BusyLabels`/`AdvanceSpinner`, the cell override and the two style
   paths. Tests: the override lands on the right column, the selected row keeps
   one unbroken highlight, `Key: nil` changes nothing, a busy row survives
   `SetItems`.
3. **containers**: a status column at 0 carrying `stateIcon`, removed from the
   Image cell; `Search` keeps matching the state. `MarkBusy` in the five action
   handlers, `ClearBusy` in `handleContainerAction`, the guard on the confirm
   path, and `BusyLabels()` rendered in the footer — which is what `pendingAction`
   was written for and never got.
4. Split `pendingAction` back into what it actually is: the confirm routing key
   only.

`datatable` gagne une **colonne de statut** et la notion de **ligne occupée**.
Suite directe de §3.21 : maintenant que les quinze tables passent par un seul
renderer, c'est le seul endroit où ça peut être écrit une fois.

#### Le trou

`handleConfirmYes` déclenche la `Cmd` et retourne **sans toucher au modèle**
(`oci_resources/results.go:17`, `containers/update.go:463`). Rien à l'écran ne
dit qu'une action tourne, et `docker/containers.go:150` appelle `docker stop`
sans `-t` : dix secondes de délai de grâce par défaut, donc dix secondes de
table qui a l'air gelée. C'est le symptôme que §3.16 a enregistré pour la modale
`"Pulling..."` du clone.

**L'intention était là et a perdu son lecteur.** `containers.Model.pendingAction`
est écrit à six endroits, dont trois phrases humaines — `"Stopping web"`,
`"Restarting api"`, `"Pruning containers..."` — et quatre tests l'affirment.
**Aucun code de rendu ne le lit.** Le champ est surchargé : il porte aussi la
clé de routage de la modale (`"confirm-delete"`, `"confirm-prune"`), que
`handleConfirmYes`, lui, lit bien. Un champ, deux sens, et celui que personne ne
lit est celui qui devait se voir.

#### La décision de forme

Deux choses partagent un glyphe et ne doivent pas partager une fonction :
**ce que l'objet est** (`running`, `exited`, `paused` — docker, au prochain
refresh) et **ce qui lui arrive** (`stopping`, `removing` — DevDesk, le temps
d'une commande). Les fusionner dans le glyphe est le but ; les fusionner dans
l'API ferait ré-implémenter la préséance dans chaque table. `datatable` porte
une règle : **occupé gagne sur l'état** — et pour une raison qui se dit, `exited`
étant précisément ce qui est sur le point de cesser d'être vrai.

**Ça ne peut pas être une closure.** L'invariant du paquet est que les colonnes
sont construites une fois et ne ferment sur rien ; un `Busy func(T) string` sur
la `Config` devrait fermer sur la map des actions en cours du modèle, ce que
`imageRow` existe pour éviter. D'où la séparation identité / état : `Key func(T) string`
sur la config, l'ensemble occupé tenu par la table et écrit depuis `Update`.

Ce que ça achète et qui compte le plus : **`IsBusy(key)` répond avant que la
ligne existe**, donc c'est aussi le garde-fou du chemin de confirmation. Rien
n'empêche aujourd'hui un second `ctrl+d` sur une suppression lente de lancer un
second `docker rmi` — le second échoue en « No such image » et l'utilisateur
voit `Action failed` sur une suppression qui a marché.

#### Hors périmètre, volontairement

Les **scans** (leur spinner est dans la colonne Scanned et ils ne bloquent pas
l'objet de la même façon) et **`prune`**, qui n'agit sur aucune ligne et relève
d'une ligne de footer rendue depuis l'état de l'opération, comme `syncStatusLine`
de §3.17 — pas de `footerInfo`, dont le timer de 3 s expirerait en cours.

A row says two things: what the object **is**, and what is **happening** to it.

m.table.ClearBusy(id)                 // on *every* outcome, failures included
m.table.IsBusy(id)                    // the guard
m.table.BusyLabels()                  // sorted, for the footer
m.table.AdvanceSpinner()              // from the view's own spinner tick

that matters most: **`IsBusy` answers for an object whose row does not exist

periodic refresh, which replaces the items mid-action.

spinner needs a `Cmd`, and this package returns none.

Rendering, and each part is a decision:

- The status cell shows the spinner **on the selected row too** — a signal that
  vanishes under the cursor is lost exactly when it is being looked at.

  column's own `Style` is dropped.

  the stored cells do not go stale as the frame advances. Tests assert on
  `View()`, not on `Table().Rows()`.

for a column carrying a `Less`, which is expensive for a glyph.

**`containers` is the first client**, and the state icon moved out of the Image
cell to get there. Two things are deliberately outside this: a **scan**, whose
spinner is in the Scanned column and which does not block the object the same
way, and **`prune`**, which acts on no row — it gets a footer line rendered from
the view's own state, like `syncStatusLine` (§3.17), because a footer *message*
expires after three seconds (Rule 128) and `docker stop` outlives that by seven.

**§3.22 est implémenté — PR #65.** Le plan est dans `.claude/plans/datatable-row-status-and-busy.md`, l'entrée backlog est écrite, et containers est le premier client.

L'API est celle dont on a parlé, avec la séparation identité/état qui était le point dur :

```go
Key: func(c docker.Container) string { return c.ID }   // nil ⇒ facilité éteinte
StatusColumn: 0
```

`IsBusy` répond pour un objet dont la ligne n'existe pas encore, donc c'est aussi le garde-fou du chemin de confirmation — le verrou sur l'objet, pas sur le curseur. Trois tests pinnent que le curseur reste libre et que le marqueur suit le conteneur, pas la sélection.

**Trois défauts trouvés en implémentant**, et le premier était bloquant :

- **`ContainerActionMsg.ID` portait le *nom*, pas l'ID.** Les cinq commandes le remplissaient depuis leur argument `name`. Personne ne l'avait vu parce que le seul lecteur était une ligne de log, où un nom se lit très bien — mais le marqueur est indexé sur l'ID, donc le message ne l'aurait jamais levé et la ligne aurait tourné à vie.
- **`pendingAction` était deux champs en un** : la clé de routage de la modale, qui est lue, et une phrase pour l'utilisateur (`"Stopping web"`) que **rien n'a jamais rendue**. Porter les deux est exactement pourquoi personne n'a remarqué que la seconde n'avait pas de lecteur.
- **La vue containers n'avait aucun timer de footer** (Rule 128). Six sites en ont un maintenant.

Deux choses que je signale parce qu'elles élargissent un peu le périmètre annoncé. J'ai touché aux tests d'action existants : ils portaient tous sur `pendingAction`, donc sur un champ que rien n'affichait — ils portent maintenant sur le footer rendu. Et trois d'entre eux exécutaient le timer de 3 s, dont **deux sur le chemin du pager, où exécuter la commande lancerait réellement le processus si le garde-fou tombait** ; ceux-là affirment l'état à la place.

Le seul point du test plan que je ne peux pas cocher moi-même : chronométrer un vrai `docker stop` de dix secondes contre un conteneur réel. C'est précisément le cas pour lequel tout ça existe, donc ça vaut le coup d'œil avant de merger.

Scans et `prune` sont restés dehors comme convenu. Les prochains clients naturels sont images, réseaux et volumes — ils n'ont rien à inventer, juste la colonne et les trois appels.
